title: Seeing Is Not Sharing: Some Vision-Language Models Overestimate Common Ground in Asymmetric Dialogue
one_sentence: Some tested VLMs confuse available map information with established referential alignment.
problem: Can an overhearing VLM distinguish potentially shared information from interpretations established in dialogue?
method: Binary interpretation matching on 13,077 references in 128 MapTask dialogues; controlled context windows and authentic, textual, blank and shuffled map conditions; detailed grid on Qwen3-VL-8B and baseline comparisons on four other models.
findings: Authentic maps improved overall performance while increasing false alignment in some models; text conveying map content reproduced the direction.
Model responses were heterogeneous: Qwen3-VL-4B became more conservative.
real_contribution: A diagnostic separating perceptual availability from grounded interpretation.
biggest_weakness: Single corpus, imbalanced labels, only 239 misunderstood cases; overhearer judgments rather than interaction.
claim_boundary: Does not establish universal VLM over-alignment, mutual belief, or failure of live repair.
why_researcher_should_care: Add alignment-specific errors and perspective controls before interpreting successful reference as common ground.
